subject: Computer Networking
title: YouTube Hijacked by Pakistan (2008)
description: A short lesson to help you apply YouTube Hijacked by Pakistan (2008).

hook.text: In 2008, Pakistan tried to block YouTube at home. Instead, they accidentally blocked it for the whole world.

buildup.text: Pakistan Telecom announced a fake BGP route for YouTube's IPs. The route spread globally in minutes.

discovery.text: Routers worldwide sent YouTube traffic to Pakistan instead of Google. The small ISP collapsed under load.

twist.text: BGP operates on trust. Any network can claim any IP range, and neighbors believe it without checking.

climax.text: The fix took two hours and sped up efforts to add RPKI route validation to BGP for security.

punchline.text: One country's censorship accidentally censored YouTube worldwide.

quiz.question: How did Pakistan accidentally take YouTube offline globally?
options: By announcing a false BGP route for YouTube's IP addresses
By cutting an undersea cable to Google
By launching a DDoS attack on YouTube's servers

details.summary: In 2008, Pakistan Telecom attempted to block YouTube domestically by announcing a BGP route for YouTube's IP space. The false route leaked globally, redirecting YouTube traffic worldwide into a black hole for about two hours. It exposed a critical weakness in internet routing trust.
details.whyItMatters: This incident showed that a single misconfigured BGP announcement can hijack traffic for a major website globally, revealing the internet's fragile trust-based routing system.
takeaways: A false BGP announcement redirected YouTube traffic worldwide
BGP relies on trust with no built-in authentication
The incident accelerated work on BGP security standards

faq.question: How did Pakistan accidentally take down YouTube globally?
faq.answer: Pakistan Telecom announced a more specific BGP route for YouTube's IP prefix. BGP prefers more specific routes, so routers worldwide began sending YouTube traffic to Pakistan instead of Google. The traffic hit a dead end and YouTube became unreachable for two hours.

faq.question: Has BGP routing been secured since this incident?
faq.answer: Partially. RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) was developed to cryptographically verify BGP announcements. Adoption is growing but still incomplete. Many networks still accept unverified routes, meaning BGP hijacks remain possible today.
